newsitem.title: USA: "Fast track" chances dimming for trade - US senators.
newsitem.headline: "Fast track" chances dimming for trade - US senators.

text.p: White House dawdling is destroying chances for passage of long-delayed "fast track" legislation to negotiate trade agreements, senators said Thursday.
"I analogize this to a closing window," said Senator Bob Graham, Florida Democrat. "There will be an even smaller bill passable in summer than now. By Labor Day, the window will be completely closed.
"There is a real cost imposed by this delay."
Three other senators complained at a Finance subcommittee hearing about administration miscues on the legislation.

Deputy U.S. Trade Representative Jeff Lang said the Clinton administration was trying to work out a "fast track" bill -- one that assures a prompt vote in Congress on trade pacts without any amendments -- with wide support in Congress. The administration has cited the consultations for months when asked when the bill would be forthcoming.
Senator Bob Kerrey, Nebraska Democrat, wondered aloud who the administration had consulted and warned that opposition was mounting to the still-unseen bill.
"I'm getting people calling me, settng up meetings to oppose something I don't even have yet," Kerrey said.
"Until the president sends something up here, he can't chastise Congress for not acting," Kerrey said.
Subcommittee chairman Charles Grassley, Iowa Republican, said the situation was lamentable in light of the long-time U.S. support of free trade.
"We're going to lose our moral authority if we don't have fast track out there as a symbol of what we believe in," he said.
Senator Max Baucus, Montana Democrat, said the Clinton administration also would have to "consult a lot more frequently than in the past" on U.S. negotiating goals.
Afterward, Lang declined to discuss with reporters where the administration stood in attempts to round up support for a fast-track bill.
"We are working with a lot of members of Congress to develop legislation that has broad support," he said.
Republican lawmakers generally want to limit fast-track authority to commercial matters. Democrats believe a broader focus, such as inclusion of labor and environmental issues, would be better.
During the hearing, subcommittee members urged a firm line in trade negotiations with China over market access for U.S. farm exports and Chinese membership in the World Trade Organization.
